newsitem.title: UK: No UK tax cuts just to win votes, Clarke says.
newsitem.headline: No UK tax cuts just to win votes, Clarke says.

text.p: British Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke repeated on Monday that he would not cut taxes simply to win votes for the ruling Conservatives at the next general election, due by May 1997.

Clarke has come under fire from some Conservative members of parliament for a weekend interview in which he rejected "frothy" tax cuts, and for saying that the Conservatives had been unable to deliver cuts promised at the last election.
Speaking from Washington, he told BBC radio: "I don't think the public would be a bit impressed by...tax cuts to win votes."
But Clarke stressed that he believed in low taxes and aimed to get the basic rate of income tax down to 20 percent from 24 percent.

"I believe in low taxation. This country is going to have a low-tax economy...It's going to have a 20 pence basic rate, but only when we firstly have a healthy economy, healthier even than now, when we've got public spending down so we can afford it and when it's good for the economy to move to it," he said.
He said electors would appreciate a politician being straightforward with them, and he hit out at Conservatives who believed the party would be guaranteed votes by cutting taxes.

Clarke said he had cut taxation in his last Budget in November 1995, albeit "less than the right-wing papers thought I ought to have cut it by", and the result was falling unemployment and rising living standards.
He said his interview had not given any hints about what his budget this November might contain.

Asked about a single European currency, he said the Prime Minister had reaffirmed the policy of leaving Britain's options open, but every time Clarke repeated that policy he was criticised by right-wing newspapers because they wanted the policy changed.

Asked if he expected to be booed by activists at the Conservative Party conference next month if he stuck by this policy, he said: "I can't help if that doesn't coincide with some newspapers, some people in my party, who wish to have a different policy."
He described such a policy as "anti-European and cutting taxes at all costs".
